selected.text: DeepH accurately predicts DFT Hamiltonians and electronic properties for twisted bilayer bismuthene with strong spin‑orbit coupling, achieving errors comparable to those for twisted graphene.

A DeepH model trained only on non‑twisted bilayer graphene structures predicts Hamiltonians for twisted bilayer graphene supercells up to ~1000 atoms with sub‑meV mean absolute error and correctly reproduces the flat‑band feature near the Fermi level at the magic angle (~1.08°).

DeepH‑E3 reproduces the band structure of magic‑angle twisted bilayer graphene (θ = 1.08°, 11 164 atoms) in excellent agreement with DFT and low‑energy continuum models, correctly capturing the flat bands near the Fermi level.

selected.text: Integrating renormalization‑group concepts with machine‑learning architectures has been used to predict transitions to canted antiferromagnetic phases in 3D Ising and Fermi‑Hubbard models, to classify quantum phases, and to recognize complex many‑body phases from raw simulation data.
Future integration of formal renormalization‑group concepts with machine‑learning architectures is a promising direction for modeling systems near criticality or with strong electron correlations.
The multiscale structural complexity measure introduced by Bagrov et al. detects phase transitions in classical spin systems via a sharp extremum in the temperature derivative dC/dT.

Machine‑learning‑driven interatomic potentials (e.g., GAP, DeePMD) and DFT‑trained surrogate models enable simulations of up to millions of atoms while retaining accuracy close to first‑principles benchmarks, making large‑scale high‑fidelity simulations feasible.

entity:meth_00144.name: Integrable Deep Neural Network (IDNN) for learning high‑dimensional free‑energy density and chemical potential functions

selected.text: Inclusion of van der Waals interactions together with DFT+U improves the accuracy of predicted order‑disorder transition temperatures for LiCoO₂ relative to earlier first‑principles studies.

The presented scale‑bridging framework, linking DFT‑informed statistical mechanics to continuum phase‑field models via IDNN‑learned free‑energy functions, constitutes the first systematic implementation of this kind for LiCoO₂ cathodes.

Integrable Deep Neural Networks trained on derivative (chemical‑potential) data accurately learn the high‑dimensional free‑energy density and chemical‑potential functions for LiₓCoO₂, achieving mean‑squared errors comparable to the reported minima and reproducing DFT formation energies with a mean absolute error below 5 meV atom⁻¹.

A Hubbard U parameter of 2.5 eV in DFT+U (with a vdW‑DF exchange‑correlation functional) reproduces the experimental average lithiation voltages of LiCoO₂ across the composition ranges {0‑1}, {0‑0.5}, and {0.5‑1}.

selected.text: DeepH accurately predicts DFT Hamiltonians and electronic properties for twisted bilayer bismuthene with strong spin‑orbit coupling, achieving errors comparable to those for twisted graphene.

A DeepH model trained only on non‑twisted bilayer graphene structures predicts Hamiltonians for twisted bilayer graphene supercells up to ~1000 atoms with sub‑meV mean absolute error and correctly reproduces the flat‑band feature near the Fermi level at the magic angle (~1.08°).

DeepH‑E3 reproduces the band structure of magic‑angle twisted bilayer graphene (θ = 1.08°, 11 164 atoms) in excellent agreement with DFT and low‑energy continuum models, correctly capturing the flat bands near the Fermi level.

xDeepH accurately predicts the band structure of monolayer NiBr2 with a 19×1×1 spin‑spiral magnetic order, matching DFT results.

The DFT Hamiltonian H_DFT({R},{M}) obeys nearsightedness with two distinct length scales: RN2 ≈ R_C for magnetic‑structure influence and RN1 several times larger for atomic‑structure influence, as confirmed by numerical experiments.

A two‑step training procedure—first minimizing real‑space Hamiltonian error, then adding orbital‑energy error at random k‑points—is essential to obtain a truly universal Hamiltonian model.

entity:meth_00229.name: Atomic Cluster Expansion extended to scalar, vectorial, tensorial properties with magnetic moments and charge transfer

selected.text: The atomic cluster expansion (ACE) is generalized to model scalar, vectorial and tensorial atomic properties and to include additional atomic degrees of freedom—species, magnetic moments, and charges—on equal footing with atomic positions.
Although the full magnetic and charge‑transfer ACE contains many parameters, hierarchical ordering of interactions allows robust and systematic fitting to reference data.

Representing tensors with spherical harmonics yields a dramatically sparser basis, where a rank‑N Cartesian tensor with 3^N components can be represented by (N+1)^2 spherical harmonics (e.g., a 10th‑order tensor requires 121 harmonics instead of 59 049 Cartesian components).
The derived ACE formulas enable efficient evaluation of forces and magnetic torques.

selected.text: M3GNet predicts phonon band structures and densities of states for SiO₂ polymorphs that quantitatively agree with DFT calculations, and the predicted phonon density‑of‑states center follows the expected ω ∝ 1/√m trend across materials.

On the MD17 and MD17‑CCSD(T) molecular force‑field benchmarks, M3GNet achieves lower energy and force errors than the Embedded Atom Neural Network and comparable accuracy to state‑of‑the‑art message‑passing and equivariant neural networks; when benchmarked against quantum‑accurate CCSD/CCSD(T) data, it attains state‑of‑the‑art accuracy for several molecules.

M3GNet molecular‑dynamics simulations of Li₃YCl₆ reproduce ionic conductivity (14.3 mS cm⁻¹) and activation energy (0.22 eV) consistent with ab‑initio MD, and short‑time MD correctly identifies known lithium superionic conductors by their high mean‑squared displacements at elevated temperatures.

For a MgO test set, M3GNet outperforms Moment Tensor Potentials in extrapolating equation‑of‑state behavior beyond the training regime and exhibits long‑range interaction characteristics similar to a Buckingham + Coulomb model.
The SevenNet machine-learned interatomic potential outperforms the earlier M3GNet model on the Matbench Discovery benchmark.
M3GNet is an extension of MEGNet model to include 3-body interactions, explicit atomic coordinates, and 3×3 crystal lattice matrix.
M3GNet achieves test mean absolute errors of 35 meV/atom for energy, 72 meV/Angstrom for force, and 0.41 GPa for stress.

The Gaussian Approximation Potential (GAP) for silicon reproduces density functional theory reference results across a wide range of observable properties, including bulk crystal, liquid, amorphous phases, and point, line, and plane defects.
The Gaussian process regression framework underlying GAP provides an uncertainty quantification that qualitatively estimates the potential’s accuracy for any given atomic configuration.

A training database of manageable size, constructed from DFT configurations covering relevant phases and defects, is sufficient to achieve high transferability of the GAP model across diverse silicon configurations.

selected.text: A cluster expansion fitted to 333 DFT‑computed LiCoO₂ configurations using a genetic‑algorithm‑guided sparse regression achieves a root‑mean‑square error of 2.49 meV per primitive cell under 10‑fold cross‑validation and accurately reproduces formation energies, especially for configurations on or near the convex hull.

The atomic cluster expansion (ACE) is generalized to model scalar, vectorial and tensorial atomic properties and to include additional atomic degrees of freedom—species, magnetic moments, and charges—on equal footing with atomic positions.
Bridging scales with Machine Learning: From first principles statistical mechanics to continuum phase field computations to study order-disorder transitions in LixCoO2
Inclusion of van der Waals interactions together with DFT+U improves the accuracy of predicted order‑disorder transition temperatures for LiCoO₂ relative to earlier first‑principles studies.

The presented scale‑bridging framework, linking DFT‑informed statistical mechanics to continuum phase‑field models via IDNN‑learned free‑energy functions, constitutes the first systematic implementation of this kind for LiCoO₂ cathodes.

selected.text: Unconstrained machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) trained on large datasets achieve accuracies on par with state-of-the-art equivariant architectures while maintaining orders-of-magnitude lower computational cost than quantum-mechanical methods.
Universal MLIPs trained on massive datasets can generalize across diverse chemical systems and can be successfully applied to structural optimization and lattice dynamics workflows.

DFT setting inconsistency between training and evaluation datasets significantly affects MLIP model performance comparisons, with PET-OMAD performing worse than PET-OAM and PET-MPtrj on Inorganic Materials due to differences in ab initio theory levels.

Central finite differences can more than halve the error for non-equivariant models on phonon calculations by averaging out inconsistencies between symmetry-equivalent displacements, and O(3)-averaging increases symmetric structures to 77% with symprec 0.01 Å in the non-conservative case.

selected.text: Training universal interatomic potential models with forces, stresses, and magnetic moments substantially improves stability‑prediction performance compared with energy‑only models, enhancing both classification metrics (F1, DAF) and regression metrics (MAE, RMSE).

EquiformerV2+DeNS (a universal interatomic potential) achieves the highest classification performance among all evaluated models, with F1 scores up to 0.983, ROC AUC 0.96, and discovery acceleration factors up to 6.33, establishing state‑of‑the‑art for ML‑guided materials discovery.
Models trained on Materials Project data systematically underpredict convex‑hull distances because the training set is biased toward low‑formation‑energy (stable) structures.

Extrapolation performance degrades with increasing WBM batch number for most models, especially Wrenformer and Voronoi RF, while universal interatomic potential models (e.g., EquiformerV2, ORB) show minimal degradation across batches.
The SevenNet machine-learned interatomic potential outperforms the earlier M3GNet model on the Matbench Discovery benchmark.

MLIP models trained on OMat24 achieve F1 scores above 0.9 for stability prediction and 20 meV/atom accuracy for formation energy on Matbench Discovery, with all five top-performing models on the Matbench Discovery leaderboard exclusively trained on OMat24.

The eSEN model achieves an F1 score of 0.925 and energy-above-hull MAE of 18 meV/atom when pretrained on OMat24, with eSEN and equiformerV2 models with DeNS outperforming their non-DeNS counterparts and all other third-party models in the Matbench Discovery benchmark task.

entity:meth_00140.name: Uncertainty-aware graph convolutional neural network for vibrational free‑energy prediction

selected.text: The presented workflow enables high‑throughput prediction of temperature‑induced solid‑solid phase transitions without performing explicit phonon calculations for each material, dramatically reducing computational cost.

Validation against experimental reports and independent first‑principles calculations confirms the robustness and predictive power of the ML‑guided framework, with reasonable agreement for transition temperatures of KNO₃, KNO₂ and CaCO₃, DFT‑calculated free‑energy differences matching ML predictions for a ten‑material subset, and thermal‑conductivity ratios for Li₄TiS₄ and NaNO₃ closely reproduced by DFT.

A graph convolutional neural network predicts vibrational free energies with root‑mean‑square errors of 8.23 meV/atom (training), 11.34 meV/atom (validation) and 12.31 meV/atom (test), and its predictions for MgS and NaH polymorphs match DFT‑computed values across the 200–700 K range.

Screening of approximately 50 000 inorganic crystals with the machine‑learning model identified over 2 000 temperature‑induced solid‑solid polymorphic transitions between 300 K and 600 K, including 130 stable transitions within the technologically relevant 300 K–350 K interval.

selected.text: Machine-learned interatomic potentials trained on OMat24 predict tightly converged DFT forces with accuracy comparable to or better than predictions for less tightly converged calculations.

MLIP models trained on OMat24 achieve F1 scores above 0.9 for stability prediction and 20 meV/atom accuracy for formation energy on Matbench Discovery, with all five top-performing models on the Matbench Discovery leaderboard exclusively trained on OMat24.

OMat24 comprises over 118 million DFT calculations across diverse chemistries, materials, and configurations for inorganic bulk materials, making it up to 2 orders of magnitude larger than other openly available datasets in terms of number of single-point calculations.

The mean absolute error between DFT predicted and experimental formation energies for 222 compounds is 55 meV/atom using OMat24 DFT settings, with compatibility corrections computed following the Materials Project MP2020 Compatibility scheme.

Training a TensorNet model on the 400 k‑structure MatPES‑PBE dataset requires approximately 15 minutes per epoch on a single RTX A6000 GPU, whereas training on the 100 M‑structure OMat24 dataset needs about 20 hours per epoch on sixteen A100 GPUs, highlighting the computational efficiency of MatPES.
Rattled systems in the OMat24 dataset have deleterious effects on model performance when evaluated on out-of-distribution hetero-diatomic systems.

selected.text: The AFLOW standard enables reproducible high-throughput DFT calculations through standardized parameter sets for k-point density, energy cut-offs, exchange-correlation functionals, pseudopotentials, DFT+U parameters, and convergence criteria.

Specific Ueff parameters are defined for d-block elements (Table 4) and U, J parameters for f-block elements (Table 5) to correct self-interaction error in DFT+U calculations, with values ranging from 1.9 eV (In) to 7.5 eV (Zn).

The first RELAX calculation is performed in collinear spin-polarized fashion with initial magnetic moments set to 1.0 µB per atom, and spin polarization is turned off in subsequent calculations if magnetization is below 0.025 µB/atom.

Electronic convergence criteria are δEelec = 10⁻⁵ eV and ionic convergence criteria are δEion = 10⁻⁴ eV for Elements database entries, while all other databases use δEelec = 10⁻³ eV and δEion = 10⁻² eV.

entity:meth_00407.name: long-range MLIP generalization framework with biased train-test splitting

selected.text: Long-range correction schemes in machine learning interatomic potentials are essential for achieving state-of-the-art accuracy, improving in-distribution performance, and enabling significant gains in transferability to unseen regions of chemical space.

Latent Ewald Summation cannot infer correct partial charges without reference charge labels and frequently predicts charges near zero or opposite in sign to reference values in challenging chemical environments such as MOFs.

Metal-organic frameworks present an ideal application for MLIPs because classical force fields lack required accuracy while DFT is too computationally expensive for large unit cells and long timescales.

Biased train-test splitting strategies including cluster, maximal separation, size, and random splits enable rigorous benchmarking by explicitly testing model performance in significantly different regions of chemical space.

MEGNet models achieve lower mean absolute errors than SchNet on 11 of the 13 QM9 molecular properties evaluated.

selected.text: MEGNet models trained on approximately 60,000 crystals outperform prior models (SchNet and CGCNN) for formation energy, band gap, bulk modulus, and shear modulus, achieving errors comparable to or better than density‑functional‑theory uncertainties.

When applied to a set of 1,585 crystals with elastic properties, CGCNN predicts bulk modulus with a mean absolute error of 0.077 log(GPa) and shear modulus with a mean absolute error of 0.114 log(GPa), demonstrating good generalization.

Graph networks (CGCNN and MEGNet) far outperform traditional ML algorithms on formation energy prediction tasks, with MEGNet decisively outperforming Automatminer for the PhDOS task; among nine structure-based tasks, Automatminer and MEGNet each achieve best scores on 4 tasks.
